utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Are interpreters ready? Registrar, could you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-14/1-T, Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Could I have the appearances for the Prosecution, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Mr. Marchesiello and Ms Erasmus for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, good morning colleagues. My name is Mikulicic and along with my colleague, Mr. Joka, we represent the Defence, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We shall therefore proceed with our case, with a witness if I am not mistaken, Mr. Meddegoda?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The witness that the Prosecution intends to call this morning is a witness whose name has been divulged to the court in the list of witnesses dated 3 March. His name appears at number 1 in that witness list. On behalf of that witness, I am seeking to apply for certain protective measures. I am seeking, your Honours, to apply for a pseudonym so that the witness's name will not be divulged. I am also seeking your Honours' permission to have the image of the face of the witness distorted during the course of transmission. I have indicated my application to my learned friend and I believe that my learned friend has no objection to this application. In the circumstances, I move that your Honours grant the protective measures that I am seeking for and on behalf of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Defence has no objection to this. The Defence agrees to these measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Turning to Mr. Gerlach to undertake all the necessary protection measures -- it is already done? Thank you. Can we please have the witness brought in and could you please close the shutters? (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, yes, I do hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. I will now ask you to read out the solemn declaration that the usher is tendering to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment so I can get my glasses. I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Let me thank you once again for coming here. You are now going to answer questions that are going to be put to you by Mr. Meddegoda, counsel for the Prosecution. WITNESS J Examined by MR. MEDDEGODA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honours? Witness, their Honours have granted certain protective measures for you during the course of your testimony and, throughout the course of your testimony, you will be known as Witness J and I also would like to inform you that your name would not be divulged and in the course of your testimony the image of your face will not be transmitted -- it will be distorted when it is transmitted to the outside world. Witness, I would ask you first of all to look at the sheet of paper that I hand over to you and confirm whether the name which appears on the sheet of paper is your name or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: If my learned friend may be shown the piece of paper and I tender it under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness J, you are a Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your religion is Islam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 26 February I was 56.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, witness, I want to take you back to the events of April 1993. In narrating those events, I do not want you to divulge any details that would reveal your identity. Do you remember the date 16 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with you at home on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son, my wife, and a neighbour also came in the morning on that day of the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time did you wake up on 16 April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I woke up at 4.30 and I did early morning prayers - "sabah".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thereafter, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, I told my wife to turn on the radio so that we could hear the news, because she was always listening to the 5 o'clock news.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you hear over the news at 5 o'clock that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard on Radio Busovaca how Dario Kordic was ordering all HVO units to attack the positions of the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell this court who Dario Kordic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dario Kordic was a man who worked at the Busovaca municipality, who before the conflict was in charge of the military affairs of -- that is, for the recruits in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his role during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the conflict, he was the chief commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of which army was he the chief commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the army of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is the army known as the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that it was Dario Kordic who was addressing over the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know -- I knew that this was Dario Kordic, because earlier, around 1990, my son was in the army and I was trying to get him out when the war broke out between Croatia and Serbia so that he would not go to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, that morning, what you heard was Dario Kordic ordering all HVO units to attack the positions of the BiH Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and to attack the positions of Bosnia Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon hearing this over the radio, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I heard this on the radio, my wife stayed in the house and my brother, myself and three or four other men went to a small forest about 200 metres away from the house and we could see down in the fields that the soldiers were already moving. Around 6 o'clock the rain started and so I went back home. They all went back to their own homes. I was there with my son, Salih, and Ramiz Zatagic came to my house. He was a neighbour of mine. He came and we were discussing where to flee, because we did not know where to go, because Kuber and Ahmici and Kratinje were all already taken, so we had no way out. I told my wife, "Go to the back room and look through the window and see if somebody is coming." We all took positions so that we could see if they were coming from the direction of Kratinje, Kaonik or Jelinak. My wife went to the bathroom. She entered the room and she said, "There are three HVO soldiers and they are carrying the Kalashnikov rifles", like this. They came straight to my house and they said, "Come and get ready." I got ready and started to go out and I asked, "What did I do to you? If I am guilty of anything, kill me now." My son was sleeping at the house. He went into the kitchen and, from the kitchen, he went to hide and, from the kitchen, he went to the pantry. One of the HVO soldiers opened the pantry door and I guess he saw his feet and so he came out of the pantry and he said, "There is no-one there" and he whispered something to the other soldier, so the other soldier walked in and said, "You - come out and get dressed, too." So then he did. Then we were all taken to my neighbour's house. So when we arrived at the neighbour's house, his son also arrived. He was born in 1969, so he got dressed as well. So, it was four of us then. We were taken down to where the mini bus was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you may be going a little fast. Your answer has to go down and the translators have to translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest you slow down because you are speaking a little too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were taken, together with your son, to your neighbour's house and could you tell this court what happened at your neighbour's house -- you and your son were taken and then you were taken to a neighbour's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened at the neighbour's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They ordered my neighbour and his son also to get dressed, so that the four of us were taken down to the intersection of Jelinak/Loncari/Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were taken to that intersection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a mini bus waiting there, and the driver of it was Mirko Plavcic, son of Jure, from the village of Jelinak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mirko Plavcic from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, because he was in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time you got in the bus, were there others already in the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we came to the mini bus, I saw inside more of our own men, who were brought there. My house was a little bit far -- a bit outside of the village, about 300 metres, so, together with the four of us, there were all together 21 persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw "more of our own men" to use your own words. Who do you mean when you say "more of our other own men"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniaks -- Bosniaks, Muslims, however you want to put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you got into the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could not all fit -- we could not all sit down, so we stood and three HVO soldiers entered and they escorted us to the Kaonik camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those HVO soldiers who escorted you in the bus -- what were they wearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the HVO soldiers and they carried Kalashnikov rifles for the most part. There were also some automatic rifles as well. They wore camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened upon reaching Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived at the Kaonik -- in the Kaonik camp, we were put in a hangar and, when I came to the hangar, I saw that there were some -- another 150, 160 other people there, who had been arrested throughout Central Bosnia. If you had a Bosniak name, you would be brought to this camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time was it when you arrived at the hangar in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we arrived in the hangar, it was about 9 o'clock in the morning -- 9, 9.15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon arrival, did you have to -- were you ordered to get off the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were ordered to get off the bus and we were lined up -- Ljubo Vukadinovic was taking down all our data; names, last names and our dates of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Ljubo Vukadinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time over there at the hangar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you first saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing a camouflage uniform with the HVO insignia. This was on 16 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After taking down your personal details, do you remember what happened to you and the other prisoners who were brought to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After they took our personal details, then they gave us something to eat. There were two or three spoonfuls of rice and some old bread -- 6 or 7 days, but it was such that my gums hurt later from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the personal property of the prisoners taken at any point in time when you were brought into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All personal effects, which we had, would -- they said, "Get up, you balijas and take out everything you have -- watches, gold and rings." Then I came and said, "Do you also want my person ID?". They said "no", but that was the only thing that I had there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son have anything with you at the time that the soldiers were searching for personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son had nothing except, in his sock, he had an ID card of the Territorial Defence. This is what he had in his sock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your son was a member of the Territorial Defence, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what type of work did he do in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in communications and he went to the village of Dvor -- this is before the conflict -- he went through Jelinak to Dvor and Putis -- some people call it Putis [pronunciation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said when you were brought to the hangar you saw about 150 to 160 detainees. Now, would you be able to tell this court to which particular ethnic group these detainees belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All these detainees were all of Bosniak ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened the next day in the camp -- that was on 17 April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the morning of 17 April, Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski entered and he said, "We need 30 men for a job", and he said that we should all line up. We all got up and lined up. They picked 29 and my son was the 30th. I could not -- I did not have a chance to come over and say, "Son, please take care of yourself" or to say, "I can fill in for him." So they were taken to either the village of Rovna or Kovacevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not asking you about Rovna or Kovacevac. You said Mr. Aleksovski came into the camp. Did he come into the hangar? Was he alone when he came into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With Ljubo Vukadinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day was it when Mr. Aleksovski and Mr. Vukadinovic came into the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was between 7.30 and 8 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what kind of attire was being worn by Mr. Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO uniform, a camouflage uniform with the patch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the physical appearance of Mr. Aleksovski to this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is a bit shortish -- shortish and he wore a hat, he had an uniform on, maybe was a bit slimmer than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise Mr. Aleksovski if you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you look around this court and say whether Mr. Aleksovski is present in this court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is he seated in this court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is over there, the last one, wearing a red tie. (Witness indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Maybe the witness could be asked to take a good look. He points in the direction of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said 30 prisoners were taken. Did you see them being taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it. They put them on to a truck, like cattle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Aleksovski present when they were taken out of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Mr. Aleksovski present when they were put into the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this group of 30 prisoners, including your son, had been taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken to the village of Rovna near Bare or maybe Kovacevac. One of those two, I cannot tell you precisely, but it should have been Rovna, because -- the place where my son dug with Rasim Kermo had features which made me believe it was Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your son and the other prisoners who were taken that morning, did they come back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean, did not all the prisoners come back or was it your son who did not come back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son did not come back and my neighbour's son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know. According to my brother-in-law --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know -- who told you what happened to your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First Sefer Osmancevic told me, because they were digging trenches -- two, three, or four men, in one place and so, as they were finishing these trenches, they would wait and -- they would wait in the vehicle, so whoever came first would come back to the camp and Sefer Osmancevic came and said that my son was wounded. He said that a bullet grazed the back of his head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you know of this incident from anybody else who had been taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard it from my son-in-law in person, who was digging trenches with him. He was wounded at 4 o'clock, and my son-in-law was trying to pull him out from the fire, so they applied bandages on it and they managed to stop the bleeding, so he did pull him out eventually and they put him in a blanket, and they brought him to the place where the car could -- a place where a car could reach. Whether it was an ambulance or some other vehicle, I could not tell, but they said that he was taken to Nova Bila hospital. Apparently, he was holding his hands like this (indicating) and he lost consciousness at that moment, according to what my son-in-law said. The person who bandaged his head said, "This one is finished", but then my son opened his eyes and he said, "I am not finished, I am still alive."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder whether it would be appropriate to have a short break to enable the witness to recover himself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. Witness J, we have a deep respect for your suffering. We will have a 15-minute break so that you can rest a little, and then come back to continue with your testimony. So, a 15-minute break. (10.32am) (A short break) (10.52am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. The witness will be brought in by the usher. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you feeling any better now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We can therefore continue. Mr. Meddegoda, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, you were narrating to this court what was told to you by -- about the incident involving your son. Do you know what had happened after your son had lost his consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put him in an ambulance, or some other type of vehicle -- I do not know, I could not tell you that, but my brother-in-law requested to be allowed to accompany him, but the HVO soldiers would not let him go with them. That is what my brother-in-law told me. Allegedly, he was taken to hospital -- whether the Busovaca hospital or the Bila hospital, I do not know, but, when my brother-in-law came back, he said that Ljubo Vukadinovic had arrived. Ljubo Vukadinovic then took my brother-in-law to Zlatko Aleksovski and my brother-in-law asked him how he was. He said he was feeling fine and I myself, I was hoping that my son was exchanged as a wounded person. This all happened on 17 April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were referring to your "brother-in-law" -- is it your brother-in-law, or are you referring to your son-in-law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother-in-law and -- it is my --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises, but it is very difficult to understand this family relationship with the witness. Could you ask the witness to repeat his answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat what was said. You said you were told about this incident involving your son. Who narrated this incident to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sidik Osmancevic was the one who told them about the incident. Then my son-in-law came and he brought his jacket to me, and gave it to me and I asked him, "Tell me the truth. Is he severely wounded? Is he going to live?". Everyone who was with him digging trenches -- everybody who came back told me that he would live, because the bullet had only scratched his head, and, according to what Sidik Osmancevic told me, he was taken to hospital by Marinko Lukin, son of Jozo from Bare. That is what Sidik Osmancevic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to ask a few questions which may tend to reveal the identity of the witness. Therefore, could we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. We will go into private session now. (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said that your son was wounded on the back of his head by a bullet. Are you aware from which direction this bullet had come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what my son-in-law told me, the bullet had come from the direction of the village of Kovacevac. He told me when he was wounded, some people were laughing at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which army was in control of the village of Kovacevac at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no -- Kovacevac at that time was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any other person who was wounded on the same day as your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know -- Ramo, my neighbour's son was also wounded -- his name was Ramiz. He was apparently wounded in the neck and it happened around 10am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how Ramo had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not tell you about that. I was not there. I just know that he was wounded in the neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, after hearing the sad news, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a parent, I could not do anything. Nobody called me at that time. I was only -- only Ljubo Vukadinovic arrived and he called my son-in-law. I could not tell you anything about their conversation there, but my son-in-law was told that my son was feeling well and that he was apparently in Busovaca or in Nova Bila in hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thereafter, do you recall seeing anything happening in the hangar on the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17 April or -- oh, yes, I know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am referring you to after 17 April -- after the day your son was shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know, I understand. In the following morning, around 4am, three young men were brought to the hangar, Saban Osmancevic, Abdulah, who we called Abdil, and Camil Osmancevic, who was wounded in the heel -- I believe it was his left heel. They sat down on a bench. We got up and asked them what had happened. They said that they were in the house of Alija Osmancevic, they had hidden there and some HVO soldiers had entered the house and started shooting around and they wounded Camil. They could not provide him with the first-aid and they wanted to take him to -- take them to Kaonik. When they brought them to Kaonik, they put them in the hangar, so on the following morning, around 8am, Mr. Aleksovski came in, in the company of a policeman, and he said, "Where are those three birds who arrived yesterday?" I heard that personally, I heard Mr. Aleksovski say that. So the doors of the hangar opened, and we were standing close to the door and we saw Saban Osmancevic take Abdulah Osmancevic, who could not walk very well and he had miner's boots on, and they took them to a Golf -- it was a police vehicle, and two policemen were standing there. They tied them up and they took them away, and we have not heard anything about them ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thereafter, did you have occasion to go to Mr. Aleksovski's office on any occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 days later, after these incidents, after my arrest, a guard opened the doors of the hangar and he asked about me and I told him who I was and he said that I should go with him to the office of Zlatko Aleksovski. I went there and got in. As I was entering the office -- whether this was Zlatko's office, or some other room or radio station, I do not know. All I know is that it was situated to the left from the entrance of the hangar. Zarko Petrovic was there. Zarko Petrovic used to visit me, because he had contacts with my son Salih, who was in charge of the local youth organisation at that time. He used to come to my house. He was on very good terms with both my sons, so they knew each other. Anyway, there was a bottle of Coca Cola there and a pack of Ronhill cigarettes on the table. He offered me the cigarettes. I said I did not smoke, but I drank a glass of Coca Cola. Then he told me, "Take these cigarettes to your colleagues in the cell." I then asked Zarko -- who then started speaking something about Kula and the futility of our fight and so on. I said, "Zarko, I am not interested to hear anything about Kula. You know what I am interested in -- I am interested to learn about the fate of my son". He said, "I can only tell you that he was wounded, and I do not know anything else about him." Zarko said, "There is nothing I can do for you. I cannot help you in any other way. I just can see to it that you are not sent to trench digging any more." On the next morning, a person by the name of

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So we had to line up. I saw him fire -- I saw him fire a burst of gunfire in the direction of the person by the name of Kovac. I do not know -- then they started taking off the clothes -- whoever had something new on him; whether shoes or a new jacket, they took away their clothes. So we had to dig until late, until 9pm, and after the work was completed, they did not want to drive us back to the hangar, but they wanted us to spend the night in a barn which was full of hay, and there were 13 of us in there and all of a sudden Mr. Zare took a hand grenade and threw it in the direction of the village of Gradine. We were afraid we would all be killed and set on fire in the barn. Anyway, on the next morning we got up and they gave us two or three cookies each and some tea. We drank the tea. After that, we had to line up against a fence. We were waiting to be relieved -- exchanged. There was a woman there by the name of Janja -- she was probably their cook. She was wearing a uniform as well. She was then told to take off that uniform, because they told her that people would think that we were conspiring with Chetniks. Then this woman came to us and she said, "I would gladly give you some more cookies, but I do not dare to. You have to finish eating as quickly as you can, but if they see me giving cookies to you, I will be killed as well."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the only occasion that you were taken for trench digging from the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When else have you been taken for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the third day, I was taken to Gradine -- this is between my village and Jelinak -- to Gradine. I went, Sadik Ribo went, Serif Pezek -- when he died, Salko, then Naib Osmancevic and Ulaga Osmancevic and the person who took us there, up to a house of a certain Fabijan, up to the fields up there. So we went and he said, "Come on, balijas, sing. I do not like you, Alija, because you are a balija, and the Drina took 100 of your mudjehadeen", so Sadik started to sing this. I told him, "Sadik, stop", but he did not hear me. Then he came back to me and he said, "So, old man, you sing now", and I said, "Sir, if I knew how to sing, I would not be here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you have to dig trenches in Gradine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We dug at Gradine from 9 o'clock until about 4 o'clock. That day we did not receive water or food -- we received nothing. When we finished this, we went to -- we started to go back to the hangar and then, when we started, he said, "Okay, sit down and take a rest." Then he said, "Whose house is over there?" I said, "It is mine." He said, "It has not burnt down." I said, "It has not." He said, "It will." I said, "Well, let it burn then." Indeed, later, it also was burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to any other places for trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were coming back from Gradine, there was another group that was waiting with Ivica Andrijasevic, who was the commander. I know he was the commander, because everybody in the unit was listening to him and he was assigning people to digging and so Sefek said, "I cannot dig any more, just kill me." He was over 62, 63. So they took us back to the hangar, and then the next time they took me to Polom -- to Polom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many prisoners were taken to Polom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 15 prisoners that were taken to Polom, but we were separated into groups of one and two, but it was great there. We got as much food as we wanted. We were given cigarettes. Your brother could not have taken better care of you. You almost felt as if you were free up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any other place that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They also took us to Podjele -- did I mention Podjele? They took us to Podjele -- this is where we spent the night. I think I said that, and then to Bakije as well. At Bakije we worked for three or four hours, so it was not much. When they brought us to the camp, it was Sunday. Mr. Aleksovski walked in, and Zarko, and they lined us up outside and he told us, "Whoever has family in Busovaca can go to Busovaca. Who does not have any family in Busovaca can go to the village of Skradno where the Bosniaks lived" and about 60 of us -- yes, it was the time when the ICRC came and gave us a couple of blankets each, and they allowed us to take these blankets along with us, and I went to Skradno, because I wanted to flee. I could not take it any more. I did not know where my father was, where my wife was, I did not know the fate of my son, so when I came to Skradno, I got information, how many people from my village were missing, but I did not want to talk about this, because I had been in a camp, so I did not know how they were pulling out of the village and going towards Kratine, but I think that somebody will come and testify to that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Now, witness -- your Honours, may I have your permission to show to the witness an excerpt of Prosecution Exhibit 4, which has been produced in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please look at the map that is on the projector? Please look at it carefully and I will ask you a few questions. You can look at it on the ELMO -- on your right. Do you see that well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see with my glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please point out, using a highlighter that is on the table, Gradine where you were taken for trench digging on the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is high ground, Gradine -- okay, this is Kozica, this is Putis. (Indicating). That is Bakije. Then Gradine, this is Podjele (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see Podjele on that map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, it is (indicating); here is Podjele.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please mark those places that you highlighted -- the village Gradine, could you please mark it with the letter "A", and Bakije with the letter "B" and, if you please, Podjele with the letter "C". (Witness marked photograph).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You may not find Polom on that map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot see it. This is Rovna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rovna can be marked as well. Rovna was the place where your son was taken to on 17 April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Could you mark Rovna with the letter "D"? (Witness marked photograph). Thank you. Your Honours, may I also have permission to show to the witness an aerial photograph, which has already been tendered in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 74. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Witness, could you carefully look at the photograph that is on the ELMO and show to this court the hangar building which you referred to where you were first taken when you were brought to Kaonik? Could you mark that building -- could you circle that building using a highlighter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the road to Kaonik -- leading from Kaonik to Busovaca -- this is the turn-off, and then you go here (indicating) and you arrive here (indicating). This is the building where the cells were, and this is where our hangar was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark the building where the hangar was -- circle that building and mark it with the letter "A"? (Witness marked photograph). So that was the building to which you were first taken when you were brought to Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the building you were detained throughout your stay in the Kaonik camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from 16 April until 13 May, and then, on 13 May, they brought us out and whoever had a family in Busovaca was allowed to go to Busovaca, and Busovaca was under the HVO control. Who did not have family was allowed to go to the village of Skradno where the Bosniaks lived. I was assigned to be with Behaija Barucija -- myself and my son-in-law (redacted) (redacted). We stayed there and beyond the village there were some fields, and we went there and the HVO police came and they asked us whether anybody was bothering us, anybody was provoking us, but my nerves were already frayed, I knew nothing about my 80-year-old father, I did not know the whereabouts of my wife, I did not know where my family was, so we decided to escape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who escaped together with you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted). We set our clocks for 1.30 in the morning and somebody gave us a shirt, some spare trousers, so we -- for 30 days we had not bathed or shaved, and so it was given to us so that we would recover a little bit. We enquired with the ICRC about an exchange, but we were in the area controlled by the Croatian Defence Council, so we did not know how we were going to be exchanged, so we decided to flee. So we set the clock at 1.30 in the morning. We got up, we all got dressed, and I started getting dressed, but all of a sudden I felt a great fear and I said, "I do not dare go," so the man with whom we stayed, he said, "My friend, it is better for you to leave. Do not wait for their knives here. The first moment I can, I will flee, too." So, I packed my bags, and we started in the area of Kaonik. We arrived at the bridge and that is where the river of Kozica was and then there is the building-block plant nearby, and my son-in-law was going first, and then Ekrem behind him and I was the last, (redacted) (redacted). I said, "If I am killed, if my son-in-law is killed, our families will be left without anyone." But I finally summoned the strength and I went along. So, at the mouth of the Kozica River in Lasva we stopped and we said, "Shall we swim across?" And I said, "I do not know." There is a main checkpoint at the Mediapan factory and above there was all HVO. I said, "I do not feel like swimming across." It was 16 May and it was still quite cold. So they had a machine-gun nest at Marica Kuce and then they ran a wire across the river, so we could trip it and it will alert them -- they would kill us all. I said, "What would you want to do instead?" He said, "I would go directly to the bridge and whatever Allah says", and I believed in Allah, if I am killed, it is fine, if I survive, thank God again. So, at Mehena Vode, a place called Korito -- there was a place where we took off our shoes and started. Around Mediapan, it was all lit. There was a little bit of fog, but it was all very well lit. We were still in the area controlled by the HVO, so Ekrem says, "I know the way. I know a path below the Mediapan." I said, "What about the mines; will there be any mines in that area?" He said, "I did not think of that." We started in the direction of the village of Strane. So we came to the first house near the Mediapan, or maybe 25 metres from the Mediapan -- this is Rezib Zatagic's house. We entered his yard and from there we went towards the house of Dzevad Sisic. Then we were now between the trenches and control point. So we climbed up to about -- to Dzevad Sisic's house and then the dog started barking. I said, "Lie down; it is the HVO patrol." So we lay in the grass for about 15 minutes and the barking stopped. Then we went through -- near a fence, and it was -- and so there was like a hedge and then it was five or six metres later, the branches started crackling, so we moved further towards the road, but we were exposed, so I held on to a branch. I did not know whether it was dry or not, so it broke on me and I tumbled over and then the burst of fire came in my direction -- about 10 of them. I lay in the grass, and I said, "Dear Allah, am I ever going to see my own?" At this point I did not care whether I would be killed or not, but I had a grandson who was two years old. "I do not know if I am ever going to see him again" -- those were my thoughts. At that point we dispersed, and we took care, each, of himself. I thought the two of them were killed. Later on they told me they believed I was killed. So, not knowing what to do, if they had moved in my direction, I would have been caught right there. I think that they did not know what it was. They may have thought that it was a bear or some kind of animal, so as it was raining, there was -- it created some kind of a run-off canal so I wanted to come to this canal and then climb up to the woods and then go through the woods, so I managed to do that. I found a path. I was on all fours. I came to the road. I looked left and right. I saw that there was a light, which was lighting the road. I went under the bushes, came into a ditch and then about 100 metres from there, all of a sudden my Ekrem and my son-in-law appeared before me and they said, "Are you alive?", "How about you, how did you manage to get through?". They said, "We went over to Vrbjce, we crossed the road and went in the direction of Lasva", whereas I followed this canal. I arrived at the gas station at Gavro and from there I crossed Lasva at the Merdani bridge, which the HVO had blown up, so I arrived there, and that is where our units were, and they were there sort of, how shall I put it, protecting that area. Two days later, another group started -- attempted to flee from Skradno and they found this -- a minefield and on that occasion Fehim and Ahmet Osmancevic were both killed and we managed to pass by there. So I went to the village of Grabe, to my sister's, and then I went to Rijeka and started looking for my wife and my family. When I saw my wife --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened? Where did you see your wife; in which village was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The name of the village was Jurevici near Babeno. That is where we met, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were united with your wife?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: was in hospital and that he would come and now it is been five years -- it will be five years on 17 April. We have not heard of him since.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: That is all your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We could perhaps have another 15-minute break before we start with the cross-examination and give the floor to Mr. Mikulicic. After that, we will go until the end of the morning session. (11.39am) (A short break) (12 noon)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, I think we have to say that, in the exhibit number 74, the witness has put the letter "E" instead of letter "A", so I think we will have to rectify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The letter "E" may stand, your Honours, or -- it could be rectified or it could remain as "E" -- I think it is phonetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: All we have to do is just to take note of that so as to avoid any possible confusion with the transcript. Witness J, you have completed your examination-in-chief -- you have answered the questions put by the Prosecutor and now you are going to answer the questions of the Defence. I believe it is going to be Mr. Mikulicic and he is going to ask you several questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor. However, before we proceed with the cross-examination, let me remind you that we would like to finish this session this morning -- we would like to finish with this witness and I would like also to ask the interpreters if they agree to prolong -- to continue working if we have to prolong the session a little bit. I can see them nodding their heads -- I believe it is okay, so, Mr. Mikulicic, you may now proceed with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have another witness, which I would like to see if I can complete this morning. He will not be a lengthy witness, but I would at least try, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my colleague, Mr. Joka, will be questioning the Witness J, thank you. Cross-examination by MR. JOKA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honours, by way of introduction, let me express the attitude of the Defence to the witness. We have also been asked by our client, who, due to procedural reasons, is not able to do it himself, to express our condolences for the difficult moments that you have been through and the difficult situation you are still in. Having said that, I will try to be as brief as possible in my cross-examination. I would like to proceed with the questions now and, in view of the contents of my questions, I would like to suggest to move into private session, because I would like to ask about certain names, and I will be referring to a witness that has been examined here -- Witness H -- so, for the protection of that witness and, also, for the protection of this particular witness, I would like to move into private session for only two or three very brief questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We will go into private session now. Mr. Dubuisson, would you ensure the necessary steps are taken? (In private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We are ready, Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Do you know the location called Bare, Witness J?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was a school building there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Could you indicate on the map exhibit number 73 the place where Bare is located? Could I please ask the usher to help me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I could, yes. (Handed). Let me see -- this is Strane -- (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with the following -- with the letter in order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which letter?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, which is our next letter -- we had "A", "B", "C" and this would be "D"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: We had "D" as well, it would be "E".

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Then it is the letter "E", yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now try and locate the village of Rovna -- we already have it, okay. What about Kovacevac, could you indicate that about the letter "F", please -- please, letter "F". (Witness marked photograph). Very well, thank you. I would now like to continue with my questions. We have finished with the map, thank you. Witness J, could you please tell the court whether you know who the commander at Bare was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander at Bare was Mr. Mario Dimitrivic -- his father's name is Mile.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me clarify one more thing. You have told the court about your meeting with Zarko Petrovic some 10 days after your son had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Zlatko Aleksovski had engaged some -- had undertaken some investigation in order to find out about the fate of your son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know -- I did not know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, when you talked to Mr. Petrovic, was Mr. Aleksovski present in the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As I was getting in, he was getting out of the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were able to speak to Zarko Petrovic freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, and also because I knew Zarko Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zarko Petrovic ask you about anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was all. He just told me not to fight in the area of Kula -- he said that it was all in vain and there were lots of trenches there, and then I told him, "Zarko, I am not interested in Kula at all. All I am interested to know is the fate of my son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what kind of function Zarko had at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose intelligence officer was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least that is what I thought. I thought he was an intelligence officer. I had contacts with an HVO policeman, and he told me that he was working for an organisation named SIS -- I do not know what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. We have completed our cross-examination and I would also like to thank the witness for his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness J, I have one question for you. If I have properly understood, Mr. Aleksovski once told you that he needed 30 people to do a job. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he came in the hangar with Ljubo Vukadinovic and he said that he needed 30 men to go -- to do a kind of job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but who said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zlatko said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Did he say anything about the kind of work that people were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not say anything about that, but it was our assumption that it would be trench digging, because there was nothing else to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay. Witness J, the court has no more questions to ask you. We would like to thank you once again for having appeared before the court. We wish you a safe journey back home to your country and we hope that the life for you is going to be better. Thank you very much?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: God willing, yes, and may I ask a question to the court, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness J, because we have no further questions for you, this means that you have completed your testimony here before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once again, let me ask you, please, could anyone tell me, if my son has been killed, where his bones lie. Enable me to bury him decently. I have been living like this not knowing anything for the last five years and the gentleman here has been accused and other persons who have been accused here -- I think that they know that, and I would kindly ask him to tell me that, if he wishes to do so. If not, very well then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Witness J, we have heard your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness does not require any protective measures and I call Daniel Damon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Do we need any protection measures for this witness, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay, you can then lift the curtains -- raise the curtains.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I speak to the Chamber? Our client, Mr. Aleksovski, has just told me that he is not feeling very well and he would kindly ask for a five minute break to collect himself a little bit? If it is possible with the court's indulgence could we have a five minute break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. We will therefore have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (12.17pm) (A short break) (12.30pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you wanted to say something about the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Not particularly, your Honours. I am not sure what the situation is entirely, but I understand that the accused has taken ill and is not able to be present. I guess there is nothing more we can do about the matter, other than simply to adjourn, unless of course the Defence are willing to proceed in his absence. I do not know whether counsel is in a position to do that or not. I understand entirely either way and, in the event that counsel is not prepared to continue, I can see nothing else but for us to adjourn. I have a witness waiting to testify, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Joka, you are very well informed of the situation as to the health of Mr. Aleksovski. We would like to hear your position in respect of that, namely, in respect of the possibility to continue the hearing or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can only say, as a lay person, that our client is really not feeling well. He has a kind of spasm and it seems like he is numb and I am told that he is being attended to by a physician right now and there is another physician on the way coming from the UN detention unit. I do not know what will happen next. We asked him whether he would be able to collect himself and to continue. He said that, right now, he could not tell, that maybe in an hour he would. Obviously, at this stage, he is not in a situation to go on. Without his presence, we do not feel that we can continue with the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes. The question is: the Rules of Procedure and Evidence do enable us to proceed without the presence of the accused, but we need his approval for that. There is also a problem here of a witness who has come to testify here today. If he does not give his testimony here today, he will have to come back. So that was my question. The Chamber can hear the witness, but we also do understand all the reasons for an adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOKA
utterances.text: I completely understand your comments. What I am trying to say is that we were not able to receive an affirmative answer from our client. My feeling is that, at this point in time, he simply does not fully comprehend our question. We appreciate the fact that there are problems regarding the witness -- I believe he arrived from England -- and he is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will consult my colleagues. Just a moment, please. (Pause). We will have to balance the interests here of the people involved in these proceedings. Mr. Mikulicic, who is the lead counsel in this case, is not present here. Therefore, I believe that it would be more advisable to finish the hearing today. We understand the problems of bringing in witnesses, but this is an exceptional situation. So, the Chamber has decided to adjourn the hearing and to continue at the end of March, as it is scheduled in our calendar. Therefore, we wish all the best to Mr. Aleksovski. We hope that he will be able to continue. I wish you a nice weekend, all of you, to interpreters, technicians, and the hearing is adjourned. (12.40pm)
